notes.h: Seasonal and geographical unemployment (Higher Level only)
notes.b: These causes come from when and where work is available rather than from the workers themselves.
points: Seasonal unemployment: jobs depend on the time of year, for example in construction, farming, tourism and hotels, which slow down in winter.
Seasonal workers in these industries are often laid off each winter and re-employed in spring or summer.
Geographical unemployment: jobs are concentrated in certain regions, so people living far from employment centres are more likely to be out of work.
Unemployment black spots are areas that lost their main employer, such as a factory closure, and keep high unemployment for many years.
Outward migration from rural areas removes working-age people, which closes shops and services and reduces the number of local jobs.
When a local firm closes, job losses spread to suppliers and services that depended on its workers' spending.

notes.h: Technical change and changing industry requirements (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Changes in production methods and in the structure of industry reduce the number of jobs available.
points: Technical unemployment: machines and automation replace workers, for example automated production lines in manufacturing and self-service banking that reduces the number of bank tellers.
Difficulty adapting: workers whose skills no longer match industry needs struggle to find new work.
Primary industries such as agriculture and fishing, and secondary industries such as manufacturing, employ fewer people than in the past, while service and technology industries need new skills.
Globalisation: manufacturers relocate production to countries with lower labour costs, removing jobs from Ireland.
Rising educational requirements: many jobs now require qualifications, so people with few or none are excluded from applying.

notes.h: Level of demand for products and services (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Unemployment rises when firms sell less, because they cut output and staff.
points: A recession reduces consumer spending, so firms reduce production and make workers redundant.
Cheaper imported goods reduce demand for Irish-made products, and the firms producing them cut jobs.
Online shopping and cheaper foreign holidays move spending away from Irish shops and tourism businesses.
Unemployment reduces household income, which reduces spending further and causes more job losses in local shops and services.
High wage costs reduce the competitiveness of Irish firms against rivals abroad, leading to lost sales and job losses.

notes.b: Residual unemployment is the hard core of people who stay out of work even when the economy is growing.
points: Causes include poor skills, long periods out of work, ill health or disability, and living in an area with few jobs.
Residual unemployment persists during economic growth, so growth alone does not remove it.
Long-term unemployed people make up much of the residual group.

notes.h: Groups who find it hard to get work
notes.b: Some groups face barriers in addition to the general level of demand for labour.
points: Travellers and ethnic minorities can face discrimination in recruitment.
Refugees and asylum seekers may not have permission to work or a valid work permit, and may lack the language skills employers require.
People with disabilities or ill health may be excluded because employers doubt their ability to do the work.
Homeless people, people with criminal records and early school leavers face employers who are unaware of their abilities, and often lack skills or qualifications.
Residents of unemployment black spots face few local vacancies and may need to travel or move to find work.

keyTerms.definition: Unemployment caused by work that depends on the time of year, such as construction or tourism work in winter.
Unemployment caused by jobs being concentrated in certain regions, leaving people in other areas without work.
Job loss caused when machines or automation replace workers.
The hard core of unemployment that persists even when the economy is growing.
An area with persistently high unemployment, often after the closure of its main employer.
The use of machines and computerised systems to carry out tasks previously done by people.
The growing integration of national economies, which allows firms to move production to lower-cost countries.
The ability of a firm or country to sell goods and services against rivals, influenced by costs and quality.

factCards.definition: Seasonal, geographical, technical, difficulty adapting to changing industry requirements, low demand for products and services, and residual.

factCards.term: Two examples of technology replacing staff
factCards.definition: Automated production lines in manufacturing; self-service and online banking replacing bank tellers.

factCards.term: Three effects of a recession on consumer spending
factCards.definition: Consumers cut spending; firms reduce output and staff; lower incomes reduce spending further.

factCards.term: Three ways rural depopulation deepens local job loss
factCards.definition: Local shops and services close; spending in the area falls; a shrinking population makes firms less willing to locate there.

factCards.term: Three reasons employers may pass over certain applicants
factCards.definition: Discrimination; mistrust of their ability to do the work; employers' lack of awareness of their skills.

factCards.term: Two examples of seasonal work in Ireland
factCards.definition: Construction work, and work in tourism and hospitality.

questions.prompt: Name two causes of unemployment that are linked to where people live, and explain how each one leads to job loss.
questions.model: Geographical unemployment: jobs are concentrated in certain regions; when a major employer closes, a black spot forms with few alternative jobs, and job losses spread to local suppliers and services. Outward migration from rural areas: working-age people leave, which closes local shops and services and reduces the number of local jobs.

questions.prompt: Analyse the causes of unemployment in Ireland, with reference to technical change and to the level of demand for products and services.
questions.model: Technical change: automation and machines replace workers, for example automated production lines and self-service banking; workers whose skills no longer match industry needs struggle to find new work; primary and secondary industries employ fewer people while service and technology industries need new skills; globalisation moves production to lower-cost countries. Demand for products and services: a recession reduces consumer spending, so firms cut output and staff; cheaper imported goods and online shopping reduce demand for Irish goods and services; cheaper foreign holidays reduce spending on Irish tourism; unemployment reduces household income, which reduces spending further; high wage costs reduce competitiveness, leading to lost sales. Each cause reduces the number of jobs available, and the effects reinforce one another.
